passages.title: A Bus Driver Goes into Politics
passages.text:
When my grandfather announced that he would run for the town council, the whole family thought he was being **silly**. “Only clever people go into politics,” my aunt said. “A retired bus driver has no chance.” Some neighbours were even harsher, calling the idea **stupid** or even **dumb**. Yet Grandpa was a **sensible** man who rarely acted without thinking, so we wanted to know his reasons.

It turned out that the new traffic rules were so **confusing** that drivers kept making expensive mistakes. “Every rule seems designed to **confuse** people,” he explained. His first speech was awkward, and several listeners looked **confused** by the long lists of numbers. However, when he described a mother who had been fined unfairly, his voice shook and he began to **get emotional**. Grandpa has always been an **emotional** person, though he hides it well. The crowd liked his honesty. Months later, he is no longer just a bus driver but a respected **politician** who still takes the bus to work.

passages.title: The New Boy Next Door
passages.text:
Mia had always been a **curious** child, and her **curiosity** often got her into trouble. When a new boy named Leo moved in next door, she watched him **curiously** from her window for days. He was **cheerful** all the time, waving to everyone and whistling as he walked to school. Mia, on the other hand, felt **miserable** because her best friend had started spending time with him instead of her.

She tried to hide her **jealousy**, but it was hard. At school she was **jealous** of every joke they shared, and she **jealously** guarded the seat next to her friend at lunch. One afternoon, Leo noticed her sad face and offered her half of his sandwich. “You look like you need a friend,” he said. Mia laughed for the first time in weeks. She realised that her bad feelings had been much bigger than the real problem, and by the end of the term the three of them were inseparable.

passages.title: Talking About Mental Health
passages.text:
Millions of people around the world **suffer from** some kind of mental health problem, yet many never ask for help. Doctors use the term **mental disorders** to describe a wide range of conditions that affect thinking, feeling and behaviour. A **disorder** is not a weakness; it is a medical condition that can be treated. Common examples include **sleep disorders**, which leave patients exhausted even after a full night in bed, and **anxiety disorders**, in which constant worry makes ordinary tasks feel impossible. **Eating disorders** are another serious group, often affecting teenagers who feel pressure about their appearance.

Some illnesses are linked to weather and daily news. Long, grey winters can **depress** even healthy people, and watching **depressing** news every evening does not help. A person who feels **depressed** for weeks, however, may need professional support rather than advice to “cheer up”. Experts say that talking openly about these problems is the first step towards recovery.

passages.title: Helen's Second Chance
passages.text:
Helen became a **widow** at forty-two, when her husband died in a car accident. The **tragedy** shocked the whole village. For months she stayed indoors, and her doctor warned that she was sinking into **depression**. Things grew worse when a legal **dispute** with her brother-in-law over the family house began. She was **frightened of** losing both her husband and her home.

Then a neighbour persuaded her to join a morning walking group. At first Helen moved slowly, but soon she was striding **energetically** along the river path, chatting to people she had never met. Slowly, her appetite and her smile returned. At the annual village festival, she even danced when the music grew loud and the crowd began to **get wild**. “I thought my life had ended,” she told a reporter, “but friends and fresh air brought me back.” The **dispute** was finally settled out of court.

passages.title: Weddings Then and Now
passages.text:
**In the past**, most people **got married** before they were twenty-five, and parents often helped choose the partner. My grandmother **married** my grandfather after knowing him for only two weeks, and they stayed together for fifty years. **Nowadays**, young people usually wait longer. My cousin Linh plans to **get married to** her colleague next spring, after living abroad for six years.

What matters most, according to my grandmother, is that two people **get on well with** each other's families. “When I moved in, I **got on well with** my mother-in-law, and that saved me a lot of trouble,” she says. She also has a funny habit of giving everyone a nickname. She loves to **call** people funny names, and she **calls** me “little tiger”. Linh says she will not follow every old tradition, but she respects the idea that a good marriage begins with kindness and patience.

passages.title: A Guide to British Money
passages.text:
If you visit the United Kingdom, you will need to learn about its **currency**, the pound, often called **sterling**. A twenty-pound **note** is accepted almost everywhere, but a single **coin** is useful for parking meters and public toilets. Most small shops now prefer cards, yet cash still matters in markets and on buses.

Before you travel, make sure your account will **be in credit**, because a bank may refuse a payment if there is no money left. In towns, most people **take out money** from a **cashpoint** on the high street. This is what British people call the machine, while Americans say **a cash machine** instead. Check the daily limit on your card, and never share your PIN with anyone. Tourists who carry a mixture of cash and cards usually have the fewest problems during their stay.

passages.title: Student Money Worries
passages.text:
Studying at university is exciting, but it can also be expensive. Many students choose to take a **student loan** to cover their living costs. Others **get a loan** from a bank when the government help is not enough. Every term, they have to **pay your fees**, and those bills can be shocking. Some students quickly **owe someone money** because they borrowed from friends for books, so they must **pay back money** as soon as their part-time job pays them.

Experts say that a small **amount of money** saved each week can prevent a lot of stress. A student named Minh decided to **save up for** a second-hand laptop instead of buying a new one on credit. “I **can't afford** a new model, and I do not want to start my career in debt,” he said. After three months he had enough, and he felt proud that he had reached his goal on his own.

passages.title: Renting Your First Flat
passages.text:
Moving into a new flat in London is exciting, but it is also costly. When Sam found a one-bedroom place, the agent asked him to **pay a deposit** equal to **one month's rent** before getting the keys. After that, he had to **pay rent** on the first day of every month. Sam had no savings, so he decided to **borrow** the money **from** his sister. She agreed to **lend** him the cash, as it was **likely** that she would not need it until her holiday in September.

Both of them knew that Sam **was likely to** repay her quickly because his new job paid well. Their father, meanwhile, had put his savings into a **certificate of deposit** at his bank, which pays higher interest if the money stays untouched for a year. “Rents **are likely to** rise again next year,” he warned, “so choose your flat carefully and read your contract before you sign.”

passages.title: Saturday at the Market
passages.text:
Saturday is market day in our town. Last week, a stall selling woollen scarves was **on special offer**: you could buy **three for the price of two**. Linh wanted only one scarf, so she tried to **haggle**. “Everyone likes to **haggle over the price** here,” the seller smiled. After a friendly argument, they managed to **agree a lower price**.

At home, however, Linh noticed a hole in the scarf. The next day she decided to **take** it **back**, and the seller offered a **refund** without any complaint. “Good customers deserve good service,” he said. Linh left with her money and a promise to return. She learnt that bargaining is part of the fun at a market, and that honest sellers will always put things right when something goes wrong. Next time, she will inspect her purchase carefully before she leaves the stall.

passages.title: A Bad Day at the Office
passages.text:
During a **tense meeting** on Monday, team leader Tom **raised his voice at** a new colleague, Anna, because she had missed an important deadline. **In the heat of the moment**, he even said that she did not understand her **job description**. The room went silent. Everyone stared at the table while Anna tried not to cry.

Later that day, Tom realised he had made a mistake. Criticism should never happen **in front of people**; a calm **one-on-one** conversation would have been far more professional. The next morning he decided to **address** Anna **about** the missed deadline, but he waited until both of them felt calmer. He knew that if he lost his temper again, it would be the **absolute last time** his manager would excuse him. Good leaders, he thought, must learn to control their emotions, especially when the pressure is highest.

passages.title: Making Peace
passages.text:
A week later, Tom invited Anna for coffee. He wanted to **have a conversation like adults**, away from the noise of the open-plan office. The café had a warm, friendly **atmosphere**, and its **relaxed** music made the situation less awkward. Tom began by saying he wanted to **apologize for** his behavior in the meeting. “I should **be mature enough to** control my temper,” he admitted. Anna listened carefully and then nodded. “I understand that deadlines are stressful. **As long as it doesn't happen again**, we can move on,” she replied.

Tom promised to speak politely in future. As they left, he mentioned a new idea: on Fridays, staff would be free to **dress** the way they want, which he hoped would create a more comfortable workplace. Anna smiled and said it was a good start. They walked back to the office together, and the other team members noticed that the tension had finally gone.

passages.title: A Walk in the Countryside
passages.text:
Last Sunday we followed a narrow **footpath** that runs beside a golden field of **barley**. The **grass** along the edges was still wet from the night's rain, and fallen **leaves** covered the **ground** under the oak trees. Some **roots** of the oldest tree had pushed up through the earth, so we had to walk carefully. A low **branch** almost hit my brother's head.

Further on, my sister, who studies biology, stopped to photograph a rare **plant** with tiny purple flowers. Suddenly a cyclist came round the corner much too fast. He had to **brake** hard to avoid us, and he nearly fell into a ditch. We all laughed with relief, and he apologised before riding away slowly. The countryside is peaceful, but even a quiet path can be surprising. On the way home, we agreed to come back in the autumn, when the colours would be even more beautiful.

passages.title: Design Class Basics
passages.text:
On Monday morning, Mr Brown's design class started with a simple task. Each student had to work with a **partner** and draw a poster. First, they used a **ruler** to **measure** the edges of the paper. If a line was crooked, they could **rub** it **out** with a **rubber**, because pens were not allowed at this stage. Later, one student picked up a **highlighter pen** to mark the main title in yellow.

The lamp on the teacher's desk would not work, until someone noticed that the **plug** had fallen out of the **socket**. Mr Brown laughed and reminded everyone that electricity can be dangerous: never touch a wet **plug**. By the end, every pair had a clear, neat poster. “Good design starts with careful preparation,” he said, and he asked each team to hang their work on the wall. The students were proud of what they had achieved together in only one lesson.

passages.title: Study Night at the Library
passages.text:
Before the final test, Hoa and her roommate Ben studied together in the library. Hoa tried to **look** every unfamiliar word **up** in her dictionary and then **highlight** the important points in her notes. When her laptop battery died, she had to **plug** the charger **in**, but the only free socket was on the other side of the room.

Hoa wanted to listen to a long recording, so she asked to **borrow** Ben's headphones. He agreed to **lend** her his best pair, and she promised to **lend** her notes **to** him next week. Ben likes loud music. At first Hoa had to **turn** the volume **up** to hear anything, but a librarian soon asked her to **turn** it **down**, and the room became calm again. Both students finished their revision late in the evening and walked home feeling confident.

passages.text:
My English class has a friendly rule: we must always **work with a partner**. Each pair has to **share** one textbook, and the teacher walks around the room to **correct my English** when I speak. If I do not know a word, I ask, “**What does** ‘reluctant’ **mean**?” Sometimes the problem is sound, so I ask, “How do you **pronounce** this word?” or “How do you **spell** it?”

After that, the teacher asks me to **repeat** the word after her three times. I also want to know how to use new vocabulary correctly, so I often ask, “How do you **use the word** ‘although’?” These simple questions help me learn faster. My partner Lan says the lessons are tiring, but she admits her confidence has grown, and she has stopped being afraid of mistakes. At the end of each class, we write down three new expressions and practise them on the way home.

passages.title: Why Is English Hard to Speak?
passages.text:
Many learners ask a teacher to **explain the difference between** ‘say’ and ‘tell’, but real progress comes from practice. Pronunciation is a good example. English has twenty-four **consonant** sounds and about twenty **vowel** sounds, so even a small mistake can change a word: ‘ship’ becomes ‘sheep’. If you want to **make yourself understood**, you must **be willing to** repeat words many times.

Writing needs the same effort. Once a week my teacher asks us to **write an essay** about daily life, and next month we will **do an essay** under exam conditions. Good students **experiment with** new vocabulary rather than using the same simple words again and again. Mistakes are a normal part of this process, and each one teaches you something useful. After several months of regular practice, even shy learners find that speaking becomes more natural and that people respond with patience and interest.

passages.title: Exam Season in Britain
passages.text:
In Britain, most students **take an exam** at the end of each school year. Some **do an exam** in a foreign language as well. The goal, of course, is to **pass an exam** with a high score, but it is not always easy. Students who **fail an exam** feel disappointed, yet they are often allowed to **retake an exam** in the autumn.

The secret is to **revise for** the test calmly during the weeks before it. Those who start early usually **do well**, even in difficult subjects such as physics. Students who leave everything until the last night often **do badly**, because they are too tired to think clearly. My cousin used to panic, but now she studies a little every day. Last summer she achieved her best results ever, and her parents were delighted. She says that a regular routine, a quiet room and enough sleep matter more than any trick.

passages.title: Study Tips from Ms Carter
passages.text:
Before her last term, Ms Carter gave her class some advice. “Always **do your best**, and **try your best** even when you feel tired,” she said. Students who want to **get a good grade** in English should **do some revision** every evening, not just before the test. In Britain, teachers talk about marks instead, so students hope to **get a good mark** on each paper.

It is also wise to **do exam preparation** with a plan: first **work on** your weakest skill, such as listening, and then check your progress. A long syllabus can seem frightening, but it is possible to **get through** it step by step. “Fifteen pages a day is enough,” Ms Carter promised. By May, the students felt calm and confident, and several of them decided to form a study group for the final weeks. They met twice a week in the library and shared their notes and ideas.

passages.title: The Morning of the Exam
passages.text:
On the morning of the national exam, every **candidate** has to show an identity card at the door. Many of them **find it difficult to** stay calm, even after months of **exam preparation**. Teachers advise students to remember that success comes from **hard work**, not just talent. A student who spends two hours a day on **revision** will understand the topics much better than one who learns everything in a single weekend.

Each paper is scored with a **mark**, and the total decides the final **grade**, from A to E. Of course, nobody can control everything. A tricky question may appear, or a pen may stop working. But **with a bit of luck**, and with a calm mind, most **candidates** will do better than they expect. Parents wait outside with water and snacks, and the whole town seems to hold its breath until the doors open again at noon.
